questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Starting a risk program
questions.question: Asked to launch a risk program at an online travel agency, a risk practitioner receives a penetration test report with 120 findings from the CIO. What should the practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Rank the 120 findings by their technical severity scores
options.B: Identify the business objectives the agency's key systems support
options.C: Choose controls for the findings that meet IT security objectives
options.D: Record each finding in the register as a separate business risk

questions.key_concept: Risk management starts from business objectives; technical findings are causes that must be tied to objectives before they are rated.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the practitioner has been handed and what is still missing.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk is the effect of uncertainty on objectives, so a risk program starts by learning what the business is trying to achieve and which systems support it. Only then can the 120 findings become risk scenarios ranked by business impact. Recording each finding as a risk is the runner-up, but findings are causes; without objectives the register fills with technical issues no owner can prioritize.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because severity scores look objective. But technical severity is not business impact; a critical score on an unused system may matter less than a medium one on bookings.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the findings need controls and IT has its own objectives. But choosing controls before knowing the business objectives and risks they protect can waste money.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the register is the core risk record. But findings are causes, not risks; they need tying to objectives and impacts before they become register entries.

tips: Eliminate: A ranks by technical score rather than business impact, and C picks controls against IT objectives before the business risk is understood.
Final two: B beats D because risk is measured against objectives; findings become register risks only once they are tied to what the business needs.
Exam cue: when a program starts from a pile of technical findings, the FIRST step is to understand the business objectives.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Evaluating an IT goal
questions.question: A hospital's IT director proposes 99.99% availability for every system. Which of the following should the risk practitioner consider MOST important when evaluating the proposal?

options.A: The business goals that require that availability
options.B: The precision of the tools that monitor availability
options.C: The business cost of that availability for each system
options.D: The availability targets set by peer hospitals

questions.key_concept: In the COBIT 2019 goals cascade, IT goals are justified by the enterprise goals they support, not pursued for their own sake.
questions.pre_read: Notice that the target applies to every system alike, then ask what each option would tell you.
questions.correct_explanation: IT goals exist to serve enterprise goals, so the first test of a uniform 99.99% target is which clinical and business goals actually need it. Cost matters, and is the runner-up, but cost can only be weighed against the benefit to a business goal. Without that link there is nothing to compare it with, and many systems may need far less.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a target must be measurable. But measurement is a later design question; it does not show whether the target is needed at all.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because near-perfect availability costs the business a lot. But cost is weighed against business benefit, which is unknown until the target is linked to the goals it serves.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because benchmarks feel reassuring. But other hospitals' targets reflect their own goals and systems, not which of this hospital's services need near-continuous availability.

tips: Eliminate: D borrows other hospitals' targets instead of this hospital's needs, and B checks measurement before checking need.
Final two: A beats C because cost-benefit needs a benefit; the goals cascade justifies each IT goal by the business goal it supports.
Exam cue: when an IT goal is set for its own sake, trace it up to the enterprise goal before weighing cost or feasibility.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Accepting residual risk
questions.question: After new controls are implemented, the residual risk of customer data exposure in a retailer's loyalty program is just inside appetite. Who should the risk practitioner confirm as the MOST appropriate person to accept it?

options.A: The marketing director who leads the loyalty program
options.B: The CISO who designed the new loyalty data controls
options.C: The risk analyst who assessed the residual risk
options.D: The platform manager who runs the loyalty application

questions.key_concept: Residual risk is accepted by the risk owner, the business manager accountable for the affected objective, not by control owners, operators or analysts.
questions.pre_read: Note each role's link to the loyalty program: design, operation, analysis or leadership.
questions.correct_explanation: The risk owner is the business manager accountable for the objective the risk affects. The loyalty program's results belong to the marketing director, so they accept the residual risk. The CISO is the runner-up because they know the controls best, but designing controls, or answering for them as control owner, gives no authority over the program's business risk; accepting the remaining exposure is the program leader's decision.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the CISO is senior and understands the controls. But designing controls, or answering for them as control owner, gives no ownership of the loyalty program's business risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the analyst knows the residual rating best. But the practitioner analyzes and recommends; accepting risk is a business decision for the owner.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because this manager runs the application daily. But running the platform gives custody of the system, not authority over the program's objectives or its losses.

tips: Eliminate: C is the practitioner, who analyzes but never accepts, and D operates the platform as a custodian rather than owning the program's outcomes.
Final two: A beats B because risk is owned by the business manager accountable for the objective; the CISO answers for controls, not for the program's business risk.
Exam cue: for 'who accepts the risk', find the business manager whose objective or program bears the loss.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. AI use case ownership
questions.question: A university's admissions office ranks applicants with a vendor's AI model, and IT manages the vendor contract. Which of the following should the risk practitioner propose as the MOST appropriate owner of the model's risk?

options.A: The IT manager who administers the vendor contract
options.B: The vendor that developed and maintains the model
options.C: The AI governance committee that oversees AI use cases
options.D: The admissions director whose decisions rely on the model

questions.key_concept: AI risk is owned by the business manager accountable for the use case; suppliers, administrators and committees play supporting roles.
questions.pre_read: Note each party's link to the model, who supplies, administers, oversees or uses it, and what each link gives authority over.
questions.correct_explanation: The risk owner is the business manager accountable for the outcome the model affects. Admissions decisions belong to the admissions director, so they own the risk, while IT, the vendor and the committee play supporting roles. The governance committee is the runner-up because it oversees AI, but a committee cannot be the one accountable person who decides on treatment and answers for admissions outcomes.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because IT manages the vendor relationship. But administering a contract gives no authority over admissions decisions or over the loss if the model ranks unfairly.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor built and maintains the model. But outsourcing moves the work, not the accountability; the university still owns the risk to its admissions.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the committee oversees AI use across the university. But oversight is not ownership; one named business manager must be accountable for this use case's risk.

tips: Eliminate: A administers a contract without authority over admissions, and B is a supplier; outsourcing never transfers accountability for the university's risk.
Final two: D beats C because ownership needs one accountable business manager; a committee oversees AI risk but cannot own it.
Exam cue: for AI risk ownership, look past builders, hosts and committees to the manager whose decisions rely on the model.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Unowned risk at committee
questions.question: At a utility, the risk committee finds a high-rated supplier risk with no owner, and a member proposes the committee own it. What should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST approach?

options.A: Record the committee as owner until a business manager volunteers
options.B: Have procurement own it as the supplier contract holder
options.C: Ask senior management to assign a business manager as owner
options.D: Keep the risk under the risk function until ownership is settled

questions.key_concept: When a risk has no owner, senior management assigns an accountable business manager; committees oversee and the risk function monitors.
questions.pre_read: Notice what kind of body is offering to own the risk, and what that body's usual role is.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk needs one accountable owner with authority over the objective it threatens, and senior management assigns accountability when no one has it. A committee oversees and challenges; it cannot be that single owner, even for a while. Recording the committee as interim owner is the runner-up because it looks pragmatic, but it leaves a high-rated risk with no individual who decides and answers for the response.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a stopgap that keeps the risk visible. But a committee is not one accountable person, and waiting for a volunteer can last indefinitely.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because procurement holds the supplier contract. But managing a contract gives no authority over the business objective the supplier supports.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the risk function tracks the risk closely. But the second line monitors and challenges; owning a first-line risk would undermine its objectivity.

tips: Eliminate: B confuses contract management with ownership of the business objective, and D puts a first-line risk with the second line, which monitors rather than owns.
Final two: C beats A because accountability needs one named person; senior management assigns owners, while committees oversee.
Exam cue: when a risk has no owner, the BEST answer has senior management assign one, not a committee or the risk function.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Skipped verification steps
questions.question: A bank pays call center agents a bonus for calls closed per hour; trained last month, they skip identity checks on one call in five. What should the risk analyst recommend as MOST effective?

options.A: Retrain the agents on the caller identity verification procedure
options.B: Discipline agents who are found skipping identity checks
options.C: Add a weekly report of skipped checks to the dashboard
options.D: Change agent incentives to also reward completed identity checks

questions.key_concept: When incentives reward behavior that bypasses controls, rebalancing the incentive addresses the root cause; training and monitoring only support it.
questions.pre_read: Before choosing a fix, note what the stem says the agents are paid for and what they already know.
questions.correct_explanation: The bonus rewards speed alone, so agents skip checks to earn it: the incentive is the root cause. Changing it, for example by also rewarding completed checks, removes the pressure that drives the behavior; the analyst recommends the change to the owner of the bonus scheme, and senior management approves it. Retraining is the runner-up, but these agents were trained last month; while pay rewards skipping the check, more training will not outweigh it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because training is the usual fix for skipped steps. But these agents were trained last month; the problem is motivation, and the bonus still rewards skipping.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it shows the rule is serious. But punishing individuals leaves the incentive in place and teaches staff to hide skipped checks.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because visibility helps oversight. But a report detects the problem after the fact; it does not remove the incentive that causes it.

tips: Eliminate: B punishes the symptom while the incentive stays, and C only detects skipped checks after they happen.
Final two: D beats A because the root cause is a pay scheme rewarding speed; training cannot outweigh an incentive that pays people to skip steps.
Exam cue: when people knowingly bypass a control to hit a target, look for the incentive and fix that first.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Pressure to change a report
questions.question: Before a board meeting, a product director asks the risk analyst to remove an unfavorable penetration test result from the risk report, saying a fix is underway. What is the risk analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Remove the result and brief the board chair about it privately
options.B: Keep the result in the report alongside the planned fix
options.C: Delay the report until the fix is complete and verified
options.D: Lower the result's rating to reflect the planned fix

questions.key_concept: Practitioners disclose all significant facts objectively; context such as a planned fix is added, never used to omit, delay or downgrade a finding.
questions.pre_read: Notice when the report will be used and who is asking for the change.
questions.correct_explanation: The ISACA Code of Professional Ethics asks members and certification holders to work with objectivity and to disclose all significant facts that, if left out, could distort the reported results. Keeping the finding and adding the planned fix gives the board an accurate, fair picture. Delaying the report is the runner-up because it sounds careful, but the board then meets without information it needs, which is the same distortion by another route.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the chair still hears about it. But the whole board relies on the report; a private briefing to one person leaves the record misleading.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the result may soon be out of date. But the board meets now, and holding back a significant fact distorts what it decides on.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the fix seems to shrink the problem. But current risk counts only actions already taken; rating as if the fix were done misstates today's exposure to the board.

tips: Eliminate: A informs one person while the record misleads the rest, and D rates the risk as if the planned fix were already in place.
Final two: B beats C because significant facts are disclosed when decisions are made; the planned fix is context, not a reason to wait.
Exam cue: under pressure to soften a report, keep the facts and add context; never omit, delay or downgrade a significant finding.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Stating management intent
questions.question: A risk practitioner at a telecom company is helping update governance documents. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate place to state management's intent that customer data is protected according to its classification?

options.A: A data protection standard
options.B: A data labeling procedure
options.C: A data protection policy
options.D: A data handling guideline

questions.key_concept: Policies state management's intent and are approved by senior management; standards, procedures and guidelines support them at lower levels.
questions.pre_read: Look at the kind of statement being made: broad intent, measurable rule, task steps or advice.
questions.correct_explanation: A policy states management's intent and direction, such as protecting customer data according to its classification, and senior management approves it so it carries enterprise authority. The standard is the runner-up because it is also mandatory, but it turns the policy into measurable specifics such as encryption strength; it supports the statement of intent rather than making it. Procedures and guidelines sit lower still.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because standards are mandatory too. But a standard sets specific, measurable requirements that support a policy; it does not state management's overall intent.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because labeling is how classification is applied. But a procedure gives task steps for staff, not management's direction.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because guidelines describe good practice. But guidelines are advisory, so management's intent placed there would not be binding.

tips: Eliminate: B gives task steps for staff and D is advisory, so neither can carry management's binding intent.
Final two: C beats A because intent and direction belong in a policy; a standard makes that intent measurable underneath it.
Exam cue: 'management's intent' or 'direction' points to a policy approved by senior management.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. New AI tool in use
questions.question: A school district has no AI policy, and its risk practitioner learns that some teachers may have uploaded students' progress reports to a public generative AI service. What should the practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Block the AI service at the network perimeter
options.B: Assess whether teachers know their confidentiality duties
options.C: Draft an AI acceptable use policy for senior management approval
options.D: Assess the exposure of student data through the AI service

questions.key_concept: When staff adopt an AI tool before any policy exists, the practitioner first assesses the exposure; policy and controls follow from it.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the practitioner knows and does not yet know about the uploads.
questions.correct_explanation: A new risk is analyzed before a response is chosen. Assessing whether and how much student data has reached the service, and what that could cost the district, tells the owner how urgent the issue is and what a policy must cover. Drafting the policy is the runner-up and will likely follow, but writing rules before understanding the exposure risks a policy that misses the real problem.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it would stop any uploads. But possible uploads are not a confirmed incident; blocking is the owner's choice after analysis, and may push use onto personal devices.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because confidentiality duties apply. But checking what teachers know neither measures the data exposure nor gives staff rules for AI tools.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the policy gap is real. But the policy should follow from the assessed exposure, so it addresses what teachers actually upload and why.

tips: Eliminate: A imposes a response before the risk is analyzed, and B checks staff knowledge, which neither measures the exposure nor sets rules.
Final two: D beats C because analysis comes before response; the assessed exposure tells management what the AI use policy must address.
Exam cue: when new technology outpaces policy, assess the risk FIRST; the policy update follows from what the assessment finds.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Continuity plan testing
questions.question: A risk practitioner at a manufacturer finds the payroll continuity plan was last tested two years ago, as a document walkthrough. What is the BEST recommendation?

options.A: Run a realistic payroll disruption exercise with the process owner
options.B: Update the plan to reflect current payroll staff and suppliers
options.C: Have the payroll process owner re-approve the plan each year
options.D: Have IT test failover of the payroll application to the backup site

questions.key_concept: Continuity plans are verified by realistic exercises with the process owner; paper reviews and IT failover alone do not prove the business can continue.
questions.pre_read: Notice how the plan was tested and how long ago. Ask what a walkthrough can and cannot show.
questions.correct_explanation: A walkthrough checks the document, not whether payroll can actually run during a disruption, and two years is a long gap. A realistic exercise with the payroll process owner tests people, workarounds and dependencies, and its gaps go to the risk register. Updating the plan is the runner-up and worth doing, but an updated plan that is still untested remains an unverified control.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because plans go stale. But updating the contents does not prove the plan works; it still needs a realistic test.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because owner approval shows commitment. But re-approving the document is not a test; it shows the plan was read, not that payroll can run during a disruption.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because system recovery matters to payroll. But failover tests the DRP for one application; it does not show the payroll process can continue.

tips: Eliminate: D tests system failover rather than the business process, and C treats re-approving a document as proof the plan works.
Final two: A beats B because only a realistic test shows the plan works; an updated but untested plan is still unverified.
Exam cue: for continuity plans, prefer realistic tests owned by the business over paper reviews or IT-only failovers.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. AI model inventory record
questions.question: An insurer's risk practitioner is inventorying the AI models used in claims, pricing and marketing. Which of the following is MOST important to record for each model to manage its risk?

options.A: The named business owner of the model
options.B: The model version and its training data sources
options.C: The platform owner and the hardware the model runs on
options.D: The business units that query the model

questions.key_concept: Every inventoried asset, including an AI model, needs an accountable business owner; classification and risk decisions depend on that owner.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the inventory is for, then test each attribute against that purpose.
questions.correct_explanation: An inventory supports risk management only if each entry leads to someone who can decide. The accountable business owner classifies the model, accepts its risk and answers for how it is used, so ownership comes first. Version and training data sources are the runner-up and should be recorded too, but without an owner nobody acts on what those details reveal about the model's risk.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because version and data lineage drive AI risk. But these details inform an assessment; without an owner, no one is accountable for acting on them.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Ratings that do not match
questions.question: A port authority's risk practitioner finds three IT scenarios, including ransomware, rated critical in the IT register but none above moderate in the enterprise register. Which of the following is the MOST likely cause?

options.A: Formal acceptance of the three risks at enterprise level
options.B: IT ratings not normalized to the enterprise rating scale
options.C: An overstated likelihood for the ransomware scenario
options.D: Transfer of the ransomware risk through cyber insurance

questions.key_concept: IT risk must be normalized to enterprise scales and rolled into the enterprise register; otherwise serious IT risks vanish from the enterprise view.
questions.pre_read: Notice how many scenarios show the gap between the registers and in which direction the ratings move.
questions.correct_explanation: When three critical IT risks all appear no higher than moderate at enterprise level, the likeliest cause is integration: IT ratings are not normalized to the enterprise scale when they are rolled into the enterprise register. wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because accepted risks receive less attention. But acceptance does not change a risk's rating; accepted critical risks stay critical in the register.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because IT teams can rate technical threats high. But one overstated scenario cannot explain why three critical IT risks all appear no higher than moderate.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because insurance is a common ransomware response. But insurance shares part of the financial loss; disruption to cargo handling and reputation stays with the port authority.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes acceptance lowers a rating, and D assumes insurance moves the whole risk; insurance shares only part of the financial loss.
Final two: B beats C because the mismatch covers all three critical risks; one overstated rating cannot explain a pattern across the registers.

options.C: The internal audit function that will later review it

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Offer to design controls
questions.question: Internal audit offers to design the access controls for a bank's new payroll system so they pass next year's audit. What should the risk practitioner advise as the BEST approach?

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the risk team is expert and close to the business. But the second line oversees and challenges; designing and owning controls belongs to the first line.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because rotating reviewers sounds like a safeguard. But it is still the audit function assuring its own design, so its independence is impaired.

tips: Eliminate: A and D both have audit design controls it will later assure; a different reviewing team does not change that the audit function built them.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Profile after an acquisition

options.B: Assess the acquired company's risks for the enterprise profile
options.C: Assess whether existing controls extend to the acquired systems
options.D: Ask the acquired company to maintain its own separate risk profile

questions.key_concept: Major business changes such as acquisitions trigger a prompt update of the risk profile, starting with an assessment of the new risks.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changed since the profile was last refreshed and what each option does first.
questions.correct_explanation: An acquisition is a trigger event: it changes the business, assets and threats, so the two-month-old profile no longer reflects reality. wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the acquired company knows its own systems. But a separate profile keeps its risks out of the enterprise view that leaders use to decide.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the profile as a fixed annual document, and D keeps the acquired risks outside the enterprise view.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Expressing a tolerance
questions.question: A bank's board states a low appetite for disruption to customer services. Which statement should the risk practitioner propose as the BEST risk tolerance supporting this appetite?

options.A: The bank will avoid disruption to customer-facing services
options.B: The bank can survive a five-day outage without failing
options.C: Online banking downtime will not exceed two hours a month
options.D: Customer service outages will be reported to the board quarterly

questions.key_concept: Risk tolerance turns broad appetite into measurable limits for specific objectives or metrics, inside the enterprise's risk capacity.
questions.pre_read: Sort the four statements into appetite, tolerance, capacity or something else before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk tolerance sets how far a specific objective or metric may move from what appetite intends before escalation, usually as a measurable limit. Two hours of online banking downtime a month turns a low appetite for disruption into a limit that can be monitored and breached. The avoidance statement is the runner-up because it supports the appetite, but it is broad and unmeasurable, so it restates appetite rather than setting a tolerance.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it matches the board's intent. But it is a broad statement with no measurable limit, so it restates appetite instead of setting a tolerance.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is measurable. But the most loss the bank could survive describes risk capacity, the outer boundary, not the limit it wants to operate within.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because reporting supports oversight. But a reporting schedule sets no limit on how much disruption is acceptable.

tips: Eliminate: B describes risk capacity, the survival limit, and D sets a reporting schedule rather than a limit.
Final two: C beats A because a tolerance is a measurable limit for a specific metric; the avoidance statement is broad and only restates appetite.
Exam cue: appetite is broad and set by the board; tolerance is a measurable limit; capacity is what the enterprise can survive.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Indicator above tolerance
questions.question: A logistics firm's KRI for shipment data at risk of loss has exceeded tolerance for two weeks, as backup logs confirm, and IT has opened a routine ticket. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Raise the KRI threshold to match the current level of exposure
options.B: Hold the breach for the risk owner's next quarterly review
options.C: Ask IT to resolve the ticket, then report its closure
options.D: Escalate the breach to the risk owner with an impact estimate

questions.key_concept: A confirmed tolerance breach is escalated promptly to the risk owner with its impact; it is a governance decision, not a technical ticket.
questions.pre_read: Notice how long the indicator has been over its limit and who currently knows about it.
questions.correct_explanation: A tolerance breach means more risk than leaders agreed to: a governance event, not just a ticket. The backup logs confirm the breach, so the first step is to escalate it to the risk owner with the likely impact; the owner can then choose interim measures or seek time-limited acceptance from the level that set the tolerance. wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the threshold no longer matches reality. But only the level that set a tolerance can change it, and moving the line to fit results hides risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it does involve the owner. But a breach that has lasted two weeks needs a decision now, not at a routine quarterly review.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because IT is already working the issue. But a fix in progress does not inform the risk owner, who must decide while risk exceeds tolerance.

tips: Eliminate: A moves the threshold to fit the result, and B holds a live breach for routine reporting instead of escalating it promptly.
Final two: D beats C because a tolerance breach needs the risk owner's decision; IT fixing the ticket leaves the owner unaware of risk above limits.

options.C: The contractor whose staff monitor the alarms
options.D: The risk analyst who tracks the spoilage KRI

questions.key_concept: Running a control can be contracted out, but its control owner stays an internal manager accountable for it working, often whoever manages the contract.
questions.pre_read: Separate the roles in the stem. Ask who answers for the risk, who does the work and who answers for the alarms working.
questions.correct_explanation: The control owner is accountable for a control being in place and working. A contractor can run the alarm monitoring, but accountability cannot leave the distributor, so it sits with the facilities manager, who runs the contract and can act when monitoring slips. The contractor is the runner-up because its staff do the work, but doing the work is not answering for the control; the warehouse director owns the spoilage risk the alarms protect.

wrong_explanations.A: The director owns the spoilage risk and relies on the alarms, but answering for the risk differs from answering for the control that treats it.
wrong_explanations.C: The contractor operates the monitoring under contract; accountability for the control stays with the distributor's manager who runs that contract.
wrong_explanations.D: The analyst monitors the KRI and challenges the control from the second line; owning it would end that independent view.

tips: Eliminate: A gives the control to the risk owner it serves, and D puts a second-line monitor in charge of a first-line control.
Final two: B beats C because outsourcing moves the work, not the accountability; the manager who runs the contract answers for the control working.
Exam cue: when a supplier runs a control, look for the internal manager accountable for it; the supplier operates, the control owner answers.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Role of an IT risk committee
questions.question: A city transit agency is chartering an IT risk committee of senior managers. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate role for the committee?

options.A: Accepting IT risks above appetite on owners' behalf
options.B: Owning the IT risks that no business manager has taken
options.C: Approving the agency's overall risk appetite
options.D: Challenging the IT risk ratings that owners report

questions.key_concept: A risk committee oversees, challenges, escalates and approves only within its authority; it does not own risk, accept it for an owner or set appetite.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a committee can and cannot be accountable for. Compare each option with who decides, who oversees and who sets limits.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk committee oversees: it reviews the IT risk profile, challenges the ratings owners report and escalates what needs a higher decision. Accepting risk above appetite is the runner-up, because committees do discuss such risks, but acceptance belongs to the risk owner, approved at the level that set the limit; a committee vote on the owner's behalf blurs that accountability.

wrong_explanations.A: Committees discuss risks above appetite but do not accept risk in place of the named owner, who accepts with approval from the level that set the limit.
wrong_explanations.B: A committee cannot be the single accountable owner. When no manager takes a risk, senior management assigns one with authority over the objective.
wrong_explanations.C: The board, with senior management, sets appetite. A management-level IT committee works within that appetite rather than approving it.

tips: Eliminate: B makes a group the accountable owner, and C gives a management committee the board's role of setting appetite.
Final two: D beats A because a committee oversees and challenges; accepting risk stays with a named owner at the right authority.
Exam cue: committees oversee, challenge and escalate, and approve only within the authority they were given; a named owner still owns and accepts each risk.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Falling security near-miss reports
questions.question: Security near-miss reports at a rail control center, such as blocked phishing clicks, fell from 30 to 4 a quarter once each counted against the reporter's performance rating. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Stop using near-miss reports to rate individual staff
options.B: Make near-miss reporting mandatory under a new policy
options.C: Retrain control center staff on near-miss reporting
options.D: Set a near-miss reporting target in performance ratings

questions.key_concept: When reporting drops after reports start counting against staff, the cause is a disincentive; protecting reporters works where rules and training cannot.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changed just before the reports fell. Ask what that timing says about the cause.
questions.correct_explanation: The drop followed a change in how reports were used, so the cause is fear of consequences, not lack of knowledge. Leaders, as owners of the rating scheme, should end the reports' use in staff ratings, protecting people who speak up and restoring the reason to report. Retraining is the runner-up: staff who filed 30 reports a quarter already knew how, and training cannot outweigh a reason to stay quiet.

wrong_explanations.B: A mandate adds a rule but leaves the penalty in place, so staff still have a reason to hide near misses or report only harmless ones.
wrong_explanations.C: Training builds knowledge, and these staff reported freely before. While reports still count against them in ratings, training will not bring the numbers back.
wrong_explanations.D: A reporting target adds a count to the same ratings that penalize each report, inviting trivial reports while serious near misses stay hidden.

tips: Eliminate: B adds a rule while the penalty stays, and D sets a count in the same ratings that punish reporting.
Final two: A beats C because the cause is a disincentive, not a knowledge gap; protect reporters before teaching them again.
Exam cue: when reporting falls after a change in how reports are used, fix the incentive; culture follows what is rewarded or punished.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Expired exceptions
questions.question: A telecom's exception register shows 30 exceptions to the patching standard that expired up to a year ago, and the systems are still unpatched. What should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST action?

options.A: Extend the 30 exceptions by a year on the owners' behalf
options.B: Report the 30 systems to internal audit as noncompliant
options.C: Ask each risk owner to renew or close the exception
options.D: Have IT patch the 30 systems before the next quarter

questions.key_concept: An expired exception leaves risk carried with no current acceptance; the risk owner must decide again whether to renew it or restore compliance.
questions.pre_read: Notice what an expiry date is for. Ask what should happen to the risk when that date passes.
questions.correct_explanation: An expired exception means risk is being carried that nobody has currently accepted. Each risk owner must decide again: renew the exception on a fresh analysis, with approval at the right level, or close it and restore compliance. Having IT patch everything is the runner-up: patching may well be the result, but ordering it skips the owner's decision and may break systems that needed the exceptions.

wrong_explanations.A: Extending exceptions for the owners is a risk acceptance made by the practitioner, who analyzes and recommends but does not accept risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Internal audit gives independent assurance; it is not the route for management to resolve its own lapsed exceptions. The owners need to decide now.
wrong_explanations.D: Patching may be the right result, but ordering it skips the owners' decision and the reasons the exceptions were granted, such as systems that break when patched.

tips: Eliminate: A has the practitioner accept risk for the owners, and B sends a management issue to the third line.
Final two: C beats D because an expired exception needs a fresh owner decision; patching may follow, but the owner chooses the response.
Exam cue: exceptions expire into a new decision by the risk owner, never into silent renewal or an order issued around the owner.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Staff delays under a new standard
questions.question: A university's new standard requires hardware security keys on all 300 systems, including dozens of low-risk sites such as the public course catalog, and staff report long delays. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Have system owners grant exceptions for the low-risk systems
options.B: Reissue the standard as an optional guideline for staff
options.C: Keep the standard and train staff to use the keys faster
options.D: Ask the standard's owner to scale the rule to system risk

questions.key_concept: Standards should be as strict as the risk requires; when a whole class of systems needs exceptions, the rule itself should be revised.
questions.pre_read: Notice which systems the standard covers and what staff report. Ask where the mismatch between control and risk comes from.
questions.correct_explanation: Standards should be as strict as the risk requires. A public catalog does not need the sign-in strength of research or finance systems, so the standard's owner should tier the requirement by system risk and seek approval through the policy process. Granting exceptions is the runner-up: it relieves the delays, but routine exceptions for a whole class of systems show that the rule itself needs fixing.

wrong_explanations.A: Exceptions suit one-off gaps. Granting them routinely for a whole class of systems leaves a flawed rule in place and builds a backlog of exceptions to renew.
wrong_explanations.B: Guidelines are advisory, so high-risk systems would also lose a mandatory requirement. The problem is the rule's scope, not whether it binds.
wrong_explanations.C: Training keeps a control that costs more than the risk it reduces on low-risk systems. Using the keys faster does not make the rule proportionate.

tips: Eliminate: B makes the requirement optional even where risk is high, and C keeps a control out of proportion to the risk.
Final two: D beats A because a rule that needs routine exceptions for a whole class of systems should be fixed at the source.
Exam cue: match control strength to risk; when exceptions become routine, revise the rule instead of excusing it again and again.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Improving a continuity plan
questions.question: A city council's continuity plan is a restore sequence for its 40 IT systems, written by the IT department. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as the MOST important improvement?

options.A: Add a recovery time for each of the 40 systems
options.B: Organize the plan around critical council services
options.C: Test failover for the ten most used systems each year
options.D: Have IT managers sign off the plan each year

questions.key_concept: A business continuity plan is scoped by critical business processes and owned by the business; restoring systems is the supporting disaster recovery plan's job.
questions.pre_read: Notice how the plan is organized and who wrote it. Ask what a continuity plan exists to keep running.
questions.correct_explanation: A business continuity plan keeps critical business processes running; restoring systems is the job of the disaster recovery plan that supports it. A restore list cannot show whether services such as waste collection or benefit payments continue. Testing failover is the runner-up, but testing a system-only plan proves that systems restart, not that council services carry on, so the scope has to be fixed first.

wrong_explanations.A: Recovery times per system refine the IT view. Without the services they support and the owners who set the targets, there is no basis for the times.
wrong_explanations.C: Failover tests check that systems restart. They cannot show whether council services continue, so testing comes after the plan covers services.
wrong_explanations.D: Yearly sign-off by IT managers keeps the plan owned by IT. Continuity needs the owners of council services to set needs and accept gaps.

tips: Eliminate: A refines a system-by-system list, and D keeps the plan owned by IT rather than by the services.
Final two: B beats C because a plan scoped to systems proves restarts, not continuity; fix the scope before testing it.
Exam cue: a BCP is scoped by business processes and owned by the business; the DRP restores the systems those processes need.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Plan after an outsourcing change
questions.question: Six months ago, a manufacturer moved its order-to-ship warehousing to a logistics provider, but its continuity plan still relies on the warehouse team it replaced. What should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST approach?

options.A: Have the process owner update the plan for the new provider
options.B: Keep the plan until its next scheduled annual review
options.C: Have the system owner retest failover of the order system
options.D: Rely on the provider's own continuity plan for the process

questions.key_concept: A process owner keeps its continuity plan current; after outsourcing, the plan is updated for the supplier, not replaced by the supplier's plan.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changed in the process and what the plan still assumes.
questions.correct_explanation: Continuity plans must follow the process they protect. Order-to-ship now depends on the logistics provider, so the plan's warehousing steps and contacts no longer work. The process owner, accountable for the process continuing, updates the plan for the provider's role, drawing on the provider's own arrangements. Relying on the provider's plan is the runner-up: it is useful input, but it protects the provider's service, not the manufacturer's process, and accountability stays with the manufacturer.

wrong_explanations.B: Waiting for the scheduled review leaves a plan that cannot work for up to a year; plans are updated after major changes, not only on a cycle.
wrong_explanations.C: Failover testing checks the order system, which did not change; it says nothing about how warehousing continues through the provider.
wrong_explanations.D: The provider's plan is worth reviewing; however, it covers the provider's own service, and the manufacturer stays accountable for keeping its process running.

tips: Eliminate: B leaves an outdated plan in place until a scheduled review, and C tests a system that did not change.
Final two: A beats D because the manufacturer stays accountable for its process; the provider's plan is input to the owner's updated plan, not a replacement for it.
Exam cue: when a process changes, especially through outsourcing, its owner updates the continuity plan; a supplier's plan never replaces it.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Recovery test result
questions.question: A lender's recovery test restored its loan system within the 4-hour RTO, yet with no process to re-enter applications taken during the outage, lending stopped for two days. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Report the recovery test as passed for the loan system
options.B: Schedule a retest of the lending process for next quarter
options.C: Raise the continuity gap with the lending process owner
options.D: Ask the system owner to shorten the loan system's RTO

questions.key_concept: A recovery test passes only if the business process continues; a process gap goes to its owner before the plan is credited or retested.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the test proved and what it did not. Ask who has to act on the part that failed.
questions.correct_explanation: The test proved the system can be restored, but lending still stopped for two days, so the plan failed where it matters. The gap belongs to the lending process owner, who decides how to close it, such as a workable procedure for applications taken during an outage, and it enters the risk register. Repeating the test is the runner-up, but retesting before the gap is closed would only show the same failure.

wrong_explanations.A: The system met its RTO, yet no loans were approved for two days. Reporting a pass credits the plan with a resilience the test disproved.
wrong_explanations.B: A retest is needed later, but running it before the process gap is owned and closed would repeat the same failure and delay the fix.
wrong_explanations.D: The two-day stoppage came from the missing process for re-entering applications, which a faster restore would not fix, and the business, not the system owner, sets recovery targets.

tips: Eliminate: A credits a plan whose process failed, and D speeds up a system that was back within its 4-hour target.
Final two: C beats B because the owner must close the process gap before a retest can show anything new.
Exam cue: a recovery test passes only if the business process carried on; any gap goes to the process owner first.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Valuing an asset for risk analysis
questions.question: Which of the following is the BEST basis for the value a risk practitioner assigns to a customer database when rating risk to it?

options.A: The license cost the business paid for the software
options.B: The book value in the fixed asset register
options.C: The cost of rebuilding the records from source documents
options.D: The business impact of losing or exposing the data

questions.key_concept: For risk analysis, an asset is valued by the business impact of its loss or exposure, not by its price or book value.
questions.pre_read: Picture what the enterprise would actually lose. Compare each option with that loss.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk analysis needs to know what a loss would cost the business, so the asset's value rests on the impact of losing or exposing it: lost revenue, legal penalties, customer harm and damage to reputation. The cost of rebuilding the records is the runner-up, because replacement cost is one part of value, but it misses the larger harms that follow a disclosure or a long outage.

wrong_explanations.A: The software license is a cost of the tool, not the value of the customer data held in it, which can be worth far more.
wrong_explanations.B: Book value follows accounting rules and depreciation. Data often has little or no book value while its loss could be severe.
wrong_explanations.C: Rebuild cost is one part of an asset's value, but it leaves out harms such as regulatory penalties and lost customers after a breach.

tips: Eliminate: A values the software rather than the data, and B uses an accounting figure that says nothing about business harm.
Final two: D beats C because replacement cost is only one part of value; business impact also covers disclosure and lost revenue.
Exam cue: value assets by business impact, not by the price paid or the book value.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Change in the data an asset holds
questions.question: A logistics firm's shipment-tracking portal, classified internal, now stores customers' passport scans for cross-border deliveries. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the portal's business owner to review its classification
options.B: Reassess the portal's risk using its current classification
options.C: Have IT encrypt the passport scans stored in the portal
options.D: Have the IT team reclassify the portal and its data as confidential

questions.key_concept: When an asset's data or use changes, its business owner revisits the classification first; risk ratings and controls follow from it.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changed in the portal's data. Ask which decision about the asset has to come before any rating or control.
questions.correct_explanation: Storing passport scans changes the portal's sensitivity, and classification drives impact ratings and handling rules. The business owner of the portal sets its classification, so the first step is to have them review it; the risk rating then follows. Reclassification by IT is the runner-up: confidential is probably the right label, but IT acts as custodian, and the owner must decide the class and accept the resulting risk.

wrong_explanations.B: Assessing risk on the old classification would understate the impact of exposing passport data. The classification must be updated before the risk is rated.
wrong_explanations.C: Encryption may well be needed, but choosing it before the classification and risk are settled puts a control ahead of the analysis it should follow.
wrong_explanations.D: IT may suggest the label, but as custodian it does not classify. The business owner decides the classification and accepts the risk to the asset.

tips: Eliminate: B rates risk on a classification the new data has outdated, and C picks a control before the risk is understood.
Final two: A beats D because the business owner classifies the asset; IT, as custodian, protects it to that class.
Exam cue: when an asset's data or use changes, the owner revisits its class and value first; ratings and controls follow.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. AI model version change
questions.question: A city council's inventory lists version 2 of a vendor's benefit-fraud AI model, the version assessed, but the vendor now runs version 3, swapped in unannounced. What is the risk practitioner's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The inventory record for the model is out of date
options.B: The model's risk rating rests on a version no longer used
options.C: The vendor changed the model without telling the council
options.D: The new version's license terms have not been reviewed

questions.key_concept: An AI model version is part of the asset; a risk rating holds only for the version that was assessed.
questions.pre_read: Notice which version was assessed and which one is running. Ask what decisions now rest on the difference.
questions.correct_explanation: A new model version can behave differently, with changed accuracy, bias or failure modes, so the council's risk assessment and any acceptance now describe a model that no longer runs. Benefit decisions rest on risk nobody has analyzed. The vendor's silence is the runner-up: it is a real vendor-management failure to pursue, but it matters because of the unassessed risk it created, which is the greater concern.

wrong_explanations.A: The stale record is how the problem shows up, not the harm. The concern is what decisions now rely on an unassessed model.
wrong_explanations.C: The missing notice is a vendor-management gap worth raising under the contract, but its result, an unassessed model flagging benefit claims, is the greater concern.
wrong_explanations.D: License terms matter commercially, but they do not affect whether fraud flags on benefit claims are accurate and fair under the new version.

tips: Eliminate: A is the record-keeping symptom, and D is a commercial matter that does not touch benefit decisions.
Final two: B beats C because the unassessed model now flagging claims is the harm; the missing notice is how it arose.
Exam cue: an AI model version is a change to the asset; its risk rating holds only for the version that was assessed.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). IT register kept apart
questions.question: A hotel group's IT department keeps its own register of 60 risks, none of which appear in the enterprise register the executive committee reviews. What should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST approach?

options.A: Send the IT risk register to the executive committee each quarter
options.B: Have the CIO accept the IT risks on the enterprise's behalf
options.C: Bring IT risks into the enterprise register in its categories
options.D: Map each IT risk to the security standard it relates to

questions.key_concept: IT risk is business risk: it belongs in the enterprise register, in enterprise categories and scales, so leaders can compare and prioritize it.
questions.pre_read: Notice who reviews which register. Ask what executives need to compare IT risk with everything else.
questions.correct_explanation: IT risk is business risk, so leaders must see it beside every other enterprise risk, rated on the same categories and scales. Bringing the 60 risks into the enterprise register lets the executive committee compare, prioritize and fund them alongside other exposures. Sending the IT risk register is the runner-up: it adds visibility, but it keeps IT risk in IT's own terms and leaves the comparison undone.

wrong_explanations.A: A separate IT register shows the risks in IT's own terms and volume, so executives still cannot weigh them against other enterprise risks.
wrong_explanations.B: The CIO can own risks to IT objectives, but accepting risks to business objectives for the enterprise takes the decision from the business owners.
wrong_explanations.D: Mapping risks to security standards helps control design, but it keeps them in technical terms instead of linking them to enterprise objectives.

tips: Eliminate: B lets the CIO accept risk for business owners, and D keeps the risks in technical rather than business terms.
Final two: C beats A because leaders need IT risk in the enterprise's terms beside other risks, not a second register in IT's terms.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Framework in practice
questions.question: A year after an engineering firm's executive committee approved a new risk management framework, what would give the risk practitioner the BEST evidence that it is embedded?

options.B: Unit managers' self-assessments of framework compliance
options.C: A crosswalk from the framework to COBIT 2019 and NIST CSF
options.D: Unit risk assessments that use the framework's methods

questions.key_concept: A framework is embedded when business units use its methods in their own risk work; approval gives authority but does not show use.
questions.pre_read: Separate evidence that leaders adopted the framework from evidence that business units now work by it.
questions.correct_explanation: A framework is embedded when units actually use it, so the strongest evidence is their own risk assessments applying its methods, scales and taxonomy. The approval minutes are the runner-up: approval by senior management gives the framework authority across units, which matters, but it shows that leaders adopted it a year ago, not that the units now work by it.

wrong_explanations.A: Approval gives the framework its authority, but it records a decision made a year ago, not how units assess risk today.
wrong_explanations.B: Self-assessments are managers' own claims of compliance. They are weaker than the assessments themselves, which show the methods in use.
wrong_explanations.C: A crosswalk shows how the framework's design relates to other frameworks. It says nothing about whether business units apply it.

tips: Eliminate: C maps the framework's design to others, and B relies on managers' own claims of compliance.
Final two: D beats A because approval gives authority, while the units' assessments show the framework in actual use.
Exam cue: evidence of use beats evidence of intent; look for the framework in work products, not in sign-offs.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Overlapping assurance
questions.question: A bank's internal audit and second-line risk team both test the same 40 key controls yearly, while neither tests its cloud controls. What should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST approach?

options.A: Agree a combined assurance map with internal audit
options.B: Have internal audit take over testing of the 40 controls
options.C: Stop the second line's testing of the 40 key controls
options.D: Ask the cloud team to self-assess its cloud controls

questions.key_concept: Combined assurance coordinates what each line tests, removing duplication and closing gaps while each line keeps its role.
questions.pre_read: Notice both problems in the stem. Check which option leaves each line in its proper role.
questions.correct_explanation: Combined assurance maps which line tests which risks, so the lines can rely on each other's work, remove duplicate testing and close gaps such as the untested cloud controls. Agreeing the map with internal audit fixes both problems while each line keeps its role. A cloud self-assessment is the runner-up: first-line checking is useful, but it closes only part of the cloud gap and leaves the duplication.

wrong_explanations.B: Internal audit gives independent assurance; taking over routine testing would replace second-line oversight and still leave the cloud controls uncovered.
wrong_explanations.C: Stopping second-line testing removes the duplication by dropping oversight, and the cloud controls remain untested by anyone.
wrong_explanations.D: First-line self-assessment adds some cloud coverage, but it is not independent challenge, and the duplicated testing of the 40 controls stays.

tips: Eliminate: B turns the third line into routine testers, and C removes second-line oversight while the cloud gap stays open.
Final two: A beats D because a combined assurance map fixes the duplication and the gap; self-assessment covers part of one.
Exam cue: when lines overlap in one place and leave gaps in another, coordinate coverage across the lines instead of moving work to one line.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Second line running a control
questions.question: For the past year, a logistics firm's second-line risk team has run the monthly firewall rule reviews because the network team is short-staffed. What should concern the risk practitioner MOST?

options.A: The risk team lacks the network team's firewall expertise
options.B: Internal audit will need to widen its review testing
options.C: The risk team cannot objectively challenge a control it runs
options.D: Rule changes made between monthly reviews go unchecked

questions.key_concept: A second line that runs a first-line control loses its ability to challenge it, and the first line stops owning it.
questions.pre_read: Think about what each line of defense is for. Ask what changes when the overseer performs the control.
questions.correct_explanation: The second line oversees and challenges first-line controls. After a year of running the firewall reviews itself, the risk team is checking its own work, and the network team no longer owns the control, so a key control has lost both its owner and its challenger. Lack of firewall expertise is the runner-up: it matters, but skills can be added, while the conflict in roles remains.

wrong_explanations.A: Expertise matters for good reviews, but it can be supplied or trained. The lasting problem is that the team meant to challenge the control now runs it.
wrong_explanations.B: Audit may adjust its plan, but wider audit testing is a consequence. It does not restore first-line ownership or second-line challenge.
wrong_explanations.D: Monthly reviews can suit the firm's risk, and nothing in the scenario shows the interval is wrong. The problem is who performs them.

tips: Eliminate: B describes a knock-on effect on audit planning, and D questions an interval the scenario gives no reason to doubt.
Final two: C beats A because skills can be added, but a team that runs a control cannot also challenge it objectively.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Control credited in the profile has failed
questions.question: Internal audit reports that an airline's access recertification control, credited in three risks the profile shows within appetite, has not operated for six months. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the control owner to restart the recertifications
options.B: Reassess the three risks without credit for the control
options.C: Keep the profile as reported until the next quarterly update
options.D: Ask internal audit to assess the control again next quarter

questions.key_concept: Current risk credits only controls that are in place and working; when a credited control fails, the affected risks are re-rated without it.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the profile credits and what audit found. Ask what the three ratings now claim that is no longer true.
questions.correct_explanation: Current risk counts only controls that are in place and working. With recertification stopped for six months, the three ratings overstate protection, and the risks may now sit above appetite. Reassessing them without the control shows the true position to the owners and leaders. Asking the control owner to restart is the runner-up: it is needed, but it does not show how exposed the airline is now.

wrong_explanations.A: Restarting the control is the owner's job and will be needed, but it does not tell the risk owners or leaders how exposed the three risks are today.
wrong_explanations.C: Holding the profile leaves leaders relying on ratings that credit a control that has not worked for six months.
wrong_explanations.D: The audit finding already shows the control has not operated. Waiting a quarter to retest leaves the profile overstated in the meantime.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves a known-wrong rating in the profile, and D waits to retest a failure that is already established.
Final two: B beats A because the practitioner first needs the true exposure; restarting the control is the owner's fix, not a rating.
Exam cue: a control earns credit in a rating only while it works; when it fails, re-rate the risk before anything else.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. AI exposure in the profile
questions.question: Several business units at a retailer adopted generative AI tools this year. Which of the following would BEST show senior management how this changes the enterprise risk profile?

options.A: AI risks mapped to the objectives and categories they affect
options.B: A count of AI tools in use for each business objective
options.C: The AI acceptable use policy and its approval date
options.D: Vendor assurance reports for each AI service in use

questions.key_concept: AI enters the risk profile as risks mapped to the objectives and categories they affect, so leaders can weigh AI exposure against appetite.
questions.pre_read: Ask what senior management uses a risk profile for. Compare each option with that purpose.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk profile shows exposure in terms leaders can weigh against appetite. Mapping the AI risks in the register to the objectives and risk categories they affect shows senior management where AI has raised exposure and how it sits against appetite. A count of tools per objective is the runner-up: it shows where AI is used, but the volume of use says little about the size of the risk.

wrong_explanations.B: Counting tools shows how far AI has spread, but ten low-risk tools can matter less than one model making credit or pricing decisions.
wrong_explanations.C: A policy states how AI may be used. It shows intent and approval, not how much risk the business units now carry.
wrong_explanations.D: Vendor reports describe suppliers' controls. They are inputs to analysis, not a view of the enterprise's own exposure.

tips: Eliminate: C shows intent rather than exposure, and D covers suppliers' controls rather than the enterprise's own risk.
Final two: A beats B because the profile reports exposure by objective; counting tools measures adoption, not risk.
Exam cue: report changes to the profile as risks to objectives against appetite, never as inventories or counts.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Exposure well below appetite
questions.question: For two years, a SaaS provider's risk profile has shown technology risk well below appetite in every category, while rivals release features faster. What should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST action?

options.A: Lower the risk appetite to match the current profile
options.B: Add controls to keep risk well below appetite
options.C: Remove controls from the lowest-rated risk categories
options.D: Report the gap below appetite to senior management

questions.key_concept: Exposure far below appetite is a finding too: it may mean excess control cost or missed opportunity, and leaders decide whether to rebalance.
questions.pre_read: Notice which way the gap runs. Ask who decides how much risk the provider should take.
questions.correct_explanation: Exposure far below appetite can mean the provider spends more on control than its risk warrants and passes up opportunities its appetite allows, a real cost when rivals move faster. Senior management should see that gap and decide whether to rebalance. Removing controls is the runner-up: it may be part of the answer, but which controls to relax is for leaders and risk owners to decide, not the practitioner.

wrong_explanations.A: Appetite reflects strategy and is set by the board and senior management. Lowering it to fit today's profile moves the limit to match the result.
wrong_explanations.B: More controls would push risk further below appetite and add cost, widening a gap that may already be slowing the business.
wrong_explanations.C: Relaxing controls could be right, but which ones and how far is a decision for senior management and risk owners, based on the practitioner's analysis.

tips: Eliminate: A moves the appetite to fit the profile, and B adds cost where risk is already low.
Final two: D beats C because leaders decide whether to use unused appetite; the practitioner reports the gap rather than cutting controls.
Exam cue: being well below appetite is also a finding; report it so leaders can weigh control cost and missed opportunity.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Input for a downtime tolerance
questions.question: Senior management asks the risk practitioner to help set a tolerance for order-system downtime at a food distributor. Which of the following inputs is MOST important?

options.A: The order system's uptime over the past year
options.B: The IT team's estimate of acceptable downtime
options.C: The business impact of outages of different lengths
options.D: The cost of moving to a high-availability platform

questions.key_concept: A tolerance reflects how much variation an objective can bear, so it rests on business impact data, not on what the system already achieves.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a tolerance is meant to express. Then compare each input with that purpose.
questions.correct_explanation: A tolerance sets how much variation the business will accept around its objectives, so it rests on what downtime of different lengths would do to orders, customers and contracts. Past uptime is the runner-up: it shows what the system achieves, which helps later to judge whether it meets the tolerance, but setting the limit from it records capability rather than need.

wrong_explanations.A: Past uptime shows capability. Setting the tolerance from it would accept whatever the system already does, whether or not the business can bear it.
wrong_explanations.B: IT can say what the system can deliver, but how much downtime is acceptable depends on harm to orders, customers and contracts, which the business judges.
wrong_explanations.D: Upgrade cost matters when choosing a response to a gap. It comes after the tolerance is set, not as the basis for it.

tips: Eliminate: B lets IT judge what the business can bear, and D prices a response before the limit it must meet is known.
Final two: C beats A because a tolerance reflects what the business can bear; past uptime only shows what the system delivers.
Exam cue: limits come from impact on objectives; capability is then compared with the limit, never used to set it.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Tolerance beyond capacity
questions.question: While helping draft tolerances for an online broker, the risk analyst finds the proposed loss limit for trading-platform failures exceeds the firm's risk capacity. What should the analyst recommend as the BEST approach?

options.A: Keep the proposed limit and monitor trading losses against it
options.B: Propose a limit within capacity for senior management approval
options.C: Have the trading risk owner accept the excess over capacity
options.D: Raise the firm's stated risk capacity to match the proposed limit

questions.key_concept: Risk capacity is the outer bound; any tolerance that crosses it must be brought inside it before senior management approves it.
questions.pre_read: Place capacity, appetite and tolerance in order. Ask what a limit beyond capacity would mean for the firm.
questions.correct_explanation: Capacity is the most loss the broker can absorb, so a tolerance above it would accept failures that could threaten the firm itself. The analyst helps by proposing a limit inside capacity, consistent with appetite, for senior management to approve. Owner acceptance is the runner-up, because owners do accept residual risk, but no owner can accept losses beyond what the enterprise can survive.

wrong_explanations.A: Monitoring against the limit would track losses the firm could not survive. The flaw is in the limit itself, and it must be fixed before approval.
wrong_explanations.C: Risk owners accept residual risk within appetite. Losses beyond capacity threaten the whole firm, which no single owner has the authority to accept.
wrong_explanations.D: Capacity reflects the firm's finances, capital and regulatory limits. It is a fact to respect, not a setting to raise so that a limit fits.

tips: Eliminate: D treats capacity as adjustable, and A monitors against a limit the firm could not survive.
Final two: B beats C because no owner can accept losses beyond capacity; the limit itself has to move inside it.
Exam cue: capacity is the outer bound; appetite and every tolerance must sit inside it, so flag any limit that crosses it.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Running above tolerance for a time
questions.question: A water utility's operations director owns telemetry outage risk and wants to run above the tolerance set by the board's risk committee for 90 days while radios are replaced. Who is the MOST appropriate approver?

options.A: The operations director who owns the outage risk
options.B: The chief engineer who leads the radio replacement
options.C: The risk analyst who reports against the tolerance
options.D: The board risk committee that approved the limit

questions.key_concept: The risk owner decides within set limits; carrying risk above a tolerance, even temporarily, needs approval from the level that set it.
questions.pre_read: Notice the roles the stem names. Ask what kind of decision the director is asking for.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk owners decide responses within the limits leadership sets. Running above a tolerance for 90 days is a temporary acceptance beyond that limit, so it needs approval from the body that set it, the board's risk committee, with the director's plan and interim measures. The director is the runner-up: they own the risk and should request the acceptance, but they cannot approve going beyond a limit set above them.

wrong_explanations.A: The director owns the risk and should make the case, with interim measures, but approving operation above a board-set limit is beyond their authority.
wrong_explanations.B: The chief engineer delivers the fix and can confirm its timing, but has no authority over the board's limits or over the risk itself.
wrong_explanations.C: The analyst monitors the risk against tolerance and reports breaches. Approving a breach would turn the second line into the decision-maker.

tips: Eliminate: B leads the fix without authority over limits, and C monitors the tolerance rather than deciding on breaches of it.
Final two: D beats A because only the level that set a tolerance can approve exceeding it; the owner requests the exception.
Exam cue: within limits, the owner decides; beyond them, take the decision to whoever set the limit.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Supplier SLA short of the RTO
questions.question: During renewal of an online grocer's warehouse software contract, the risk analyst finds its restoration SLA is 24 hours, against an 8-hour business RTO for dispatch. What is the BEST recommendation?

options.A: Have the contract owner negotiate an SLA that meets the RTO
options.B: Accept the SLA and rely on service credits for missed targets
options.C: Change the dispatch RTO to 24 hours to match the contract
options.D: Have the contract owner add a right-to-audit clause

questions.key_concept: Supplier SLAs must meet business recovery needs; service credits shift part of the cost, while the impact and accountability stay with the enterprise.
questions.pre_read: Compare the two numbers and ask which one should give way. Then ask what each option does to the gap.
questions.correct_explanation: Supplier terms should meet the business's recovery need, and renewal is when the grocer has leverage to fix them. The contract owner should negotiate restoration within the 8-hour RTO; if the provider cannot meet it, the business owner decides on a workaround or accepts the gap. Relying on service credits is the runner-up: credits repay part of the fee, but dispatch still stops and the grocer keeps the impact.

wrong_explanations.B: Service credits repay part of the fee after a miss. They do not restore dispatch within 8 hours, and the grocer still bears the lost orders.
wrong_explanations.C: The RTO reflects how long dispatch can be down before harm becomes unacceptable. Moving it to fit the contract hides the gap instead of closing it.
wrong_explanations.D: Audit rights help verify the provider's controls, but they leave the 24-hour restoration target unchanged and the gap open.

tips: Eliminate: C bends the business need to fit the contract, and D adds oversight without changing the restoration target.
Final two: A beats B because credits shift part of the cost, not the impact; the contract must meet the business's recovery need.
Exam cue: supplier SLAs serve business recovery targets; outsourcing moves the work, never the accountability for the outcome.

tips: Eliminate: B adopts another organization's priorities, and D lets audit attention set them in place of risk.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. New AI law
questions.question: A staffing agency plans to screen applicants with an AI model, and a law taking effect in nine months will class that use as high-risk. What is the risk practitioner's BEST course of action?

options.A: Ask the vendor to certify that the model meets the law
options.B: Assess the law's impact on the planned screening use
options.C: Wait for the regulator's guidance before assessing it
options.D: Recommend that the agency cancel the screening project

questions.key_concept: A new legal obligation is a source of risk: assess its impact on the planned use before its effective date, before relying on vendor assurance.
questions.pre_read: Notice how much time remains before the law applies. Ask what the agency must know before choosing any response.
questions.correct_explanation: A new obligation is a source of risk, and nine months is the time to understand it. Assessing the law's impact on the planned screening use shows which duties fall on the agency, such as oversight, testing or records, and who should own them. A vendor certificate is the runner-up: it can be useful evidence, but many duties fall on the system's user, and the agency cannot judge a certificate until it knows them.

wrong_explanations.A: A vendor's certificate covers the model, not how the agency will use it. The agency first needs to know its own duties as the user of a high-risk system.
wrong_explanations.C: Guidance may refine details, but waiting shortens the time left to meet duties that are already known. The impact assessment can start now.
wrong_explanations.D: Cancelling is an avoidance response chosen before the risk is analyzed. The business decides once the impact and options are clear.

tips: Eliminate: C delays analysis the effective date makes pressing, and D chooses avoidance before the risk is known.
Final two: B beats A because the agency must know its own duties as the user before a vendor's certificate can show they are met.
Exam cue: a new law or rule triggers an impact assessment before its effective date; apply the principle, not a quoted clause.
